title: The zero scheme of a geometrically semisimple derivation of a smooth affine algebra is smooth
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $\bar k$ be an algebraic closure [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $A$ be a commutative finite-type $k$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] for which $\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] is smooth over $k$ [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Let $D:A\to A$ be a $k$-linear derivation, meaning $D(ab)=aD(b)+D(a)b$ for all $a,b\in A$. Suppose that on $A_{\bar k}=A\otimes_k\bar k$ the scalar-extended derivation $D_{\bar k}=D\otimes1$ admits an eigenspace decomposition $$A_{\bar k}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\bar k}\ker(D_{\bar k}-\lambda\,\mathrm{id}),$$ where each vector has finitely many nonzero components. Let $I=(D(a):a\in A)\subseteq A$ be the ideal generated by the values of $D$. Then the closed zero subscheme $\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-closed-immersion] is smooth over $k$. The zero algebra, the zero derivation, arbitrary characteristic, and imperfect $k$ are allowed.

source.place: Proposition 17.76, printed p.377: the modification of Lemma 13.6 that its proof leaves implicit, with Lemma 13.3, printed p.255, for the regular local quotient. This general derivation formulation is an agent-stated prerequisite to that argument, not a separately numbered theorem in Milne.

proof.text: Put $K=\bar k$, $A_K=A\otimes_kK$, $D_K=D\otimes1$, and $I_K=IA_K$. The values $D_K(\sum a_i\otimes c_i)=\sum D(a_i)\otimes c_i$ generate exactly $I_K$: one inclusion follows from this formula and the other from $D_K(a\otimes1)=D(a)\otimes1$. Tensor-quotient base change gives $(A/I)\otimes_kK\cong A_K/I_K$, and affine fibre products identify its spectrum with the base change of the asserted zero scheme. The affine smoothness equivalence and smooth ring-map base change show that $\operatorname{Spec}A_K$ is smooth over $K$. Finite algebra generators of $A$ give finite algebra generators after this base change and after taking any quotient. We first prove the assertion over $K$, where the assumed decomposition is available; descent back to the original $k$ is step 10.

source.place: Tags 00DF (lemma-tensor-product-exact) and 00T4 (lemma-base-change-smooth); the equality of derivation ideals is the displayed direct calculation

proof.text: For steps 2--9 rename $K,A_K,D_K,I_K$ as $k,A,D,I$; thus $k$ is algebraically closed and $D$ is diagonalizable on $A$. Fix a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supseteq I$ and put $R=A_{\mathfrak m}$ and $\mathfrak n=\mathfrak mR$. The closed-point residue-field statement identifies $A/\mathfrak m=R/\mathfrak n=k$. By the affine smoothness equivalence $A$ is a smooth $k$-algebra, so the smooth-over-field regular-local statement gives that $R$ is regular local. In particular $R$ is Noetherian, $\mathfrak n$ is finitely generated, and $V=\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2$ has finite dimension $d$ over $k$. If there is no such maximal ideal then $A/I=0$; the empty spectrum is included in the covering argument in step 9.

source.place: Tags 00FV (theorem-nullstellensatz) and 00TT (lemma-characterize-smooth-over-field); Milne 13.2, printed p.254, regular local convention

proof.text: Extend $D$ to $R$ by the localization lemma: $\delta(a/b)=D(a)/b-aD(b)/b^2$. Write $L=IR$. The displayed formula proves $L=(\delta(r):r\in R)$, since every $D(a)/1=\delta(a/1)$ and every $\delta(a/b)$ belongs to $IR$. We have $\delta(R)\subseteq L\subseteq\mathfrak n$, hence $\delta(\mathfrak n)\subseteq\mathfrak n$ and the product rule gives $\delta(\mathfrak n^q)\subseteq\mathfrak n^q$ for every $q\geq1$. Also $D(\mathfrak m)\subseteq I\subseteq\mathfrak m$, so the global ideal $\mathfrak m$ is $D$-stable. Thus $\delta$ acts on $V$. The quotient local ring of $A/I$ at $\mathfrak m/I$ is $R/L$: the inverse identifications send $(a+I)/(b+I)$ to $a/b+L$, for $b\notin\mathfrak m$, and back by the same fraction formula; the fraction equality relations are preserved in both directions.

source.place: Tag 07PE (lemma-derivation-extends), part (2); the equality of ideals and quotient fraction maps are written out here

proof.text: There are global eigenvectors $x_1,\ldots,x_d\in\mathfrak m$ whose images form a $k$-basis of $V$. Here is the linear-algebra argument. The map $\mathfrak m\to V$ is surjective: for $a/b\in\mathfrak n$, take $a\in\mathfrak m$ and write $b=c+h$ with $c\in k^\times$, $h\in\mathfrak m$; then $a/b\equiv c^{-1}a\pmod{\mathfrak n^2}$. Decompose each of finitely many lifts of a basis of $V$ into its finitely many $D$-eigencomponents. Each component is still in $\mathfrak m$: on the finite set $F$ of eigenvalues occurring in that lift, its $\lambda$-component equals $\prod_{\mu\in F\setminus\{\lambda\}}(D-\mu)/(\lambda-\mu)$ applied to the lift, and $\mathfrak m$ is $D$-stable. Their images in $V$ are eigenvectors and span $V$, so select a basis among these images. Let $D(x_i)=\lambda_i x_i$ and order the chosen basis so that $\lambda_i\ne0$ precisely for $1\leq i\leq s$. Only differences of distinct eigenvalues are inverted, which is valid in every characteristic.

source.place: Proposition 17.76, printed p.377: decomposition of the cotangent space in the modification of Lemma 13.6; finite spectral projectors and global eigenvector lifts supplied explicitly by the agent

proof.text: The images of the $x_i$ in $R$ generate $\mathfrak n$. Indeed apply the cited Nakayama statement with the local ring $R$, the finitely generated $R$-module $M=\mathfrak n$, and the chosen elements $x_i$. Their images are a basis of $M/\mathfrak nM=\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2$, so they generate $M$. This also treats $d=0$, when $\mathfrak n=0$.

For every $N\geq1$, each element of $R/\mathfrak n^{N+1}$ is represented by a polynomial in the $x_i$ with coefficients in $k$. Explicitly, for $r\in R$ subtract its residue $c_0\in k$ to obtain an element of $\mathfrak n=(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$. More generally, if a residual error lies in $\mathfrak n^q$, express it as a sum of degree-$q$ monomials in the $x_i$ with coefficients in $R$, and replace each coefficient by its residue in $k$; the new error lies in $\mathfrak n^{q+1}$. Starting at $q=1$ and repeating through $q=N$ proves the assertion. This finite induction uses no completion, convergence, or division by positive integers.

source.place: Proof of Lemma 13.6, printed p.256: generation modulo powers of the maximal ideal; the finite monomial expansion used in the derivation version is written out

proof.text: Put $J=(x_1,\ldots,x_s)R$. Since $\lambda_i\ne0$ for $i\leq s$, the identity $x_i=\lambda_i^{-1}\delta(x_i)$ gives $J\subseteq L$. Conversely, $\delta$ sends every polynomial in the $x_i$ into $J$: on a monomial $x_1^{e_1}\cdots x_d^{e_d}$ its value is $(\sum_i e_i\lambda_i)x_1^{e_1}\cdots x_d^{e_d}$. If any $e_i>0$ with $i\leq s$, the monomial belongs to $J$; otherwise the sum is zero. For $r\in R$, choose the polynomial representative modulo $\mathfrak n^{N+1}$ from step 6. Step 3 gives $\delta(r)\in J+\mathfrak n^{N+1}$. Since $L$ is generated by these values, $L\subseteq J+\mathfrak n^{N+1}$. Therefore, for every $N\geq1$, $$L+\mathfrak n^{N+1}=(x_1,\ldots,x_s)R+\mathfrak n^{N+1}.$$ This argument remains valid when nonzero eigenvalues have sums equal to zero in positive characteristic.

source.place: Proposition 17.76, printed p.377, modification of Lemma 13.6, printed p.256: the derivation-ideal calculation replacing differences of automorphisms

proof.text: Apply the cited regular-quotient approximation criterion to the regular local ring $(R,\mathfrak n)$, the ideal $L\subseteq\mathfrak n$, and the fixed integer $s$, with the same tuple $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$ for every $N$. Its cotangent-basis hypothesis is step 4 and its ideal equality for every $N\geq1$ is step 7. It follows that $R/L$ is regular local, of dimension $d-s$. Through the fraction isomorphism in step 3, the local ring $(A/I)_{\mathfrak m/I}$ is therefore regular. No regularity assertion about a quotient has been assumed before this application.

source.place: Lemma 13.3, printed p.255 (including the empty subset of parameters)
Tag 00TS (lemma-characterize-smooth-kbar), implication (1) to (4); Morphisms Tag 01V6 (lemma-smooth-characterize), locality on source

proof.text: Return to the original field $k$ and $K=\bar k$. Steps 2--9 prove that $\operatorname{Spec}(A_K/I_K)$ is smooth over $K$; step 1 identifies it with the base change of $\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$. The morphism $\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is flat by the field-flatness statement, surjective because both spectra have one point, and quasi-compact because its source has one point. The cited fpqc descent statement now proves smoothness of $\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$ over $k$. This proves the assertion also for imperfect $k$. For $D=0$ the construction has $s=0$ and $I=0$; for the zero algebra or for $I=A$ its zero scheme is empty, already handled in step 9.
